title: After September 2001
hook: Balbir Singh Sodhi, a Sikh gas station owner in Arizona, is killed in a hate crime

segments.voice: Yesterday, dastar: a schoolboy in Birmingham, a police officer in Canada, and your line, the right to be yourself. Today, what happened to that right in America in the days after a national tragedy. Go gently. Day three hundred twenty.

Mesa, Arizona. Saturday, September fifteenth, 2001, four days after the attacks of September eleventh. The whole country is grieving and afraid. Outside his gas station, a man named Balbir Singh Sodhi is helping a landscaper plant flowers around the sign. Earlier that week, he'd donated to a fund for the victims. He wears a turban and a beard, as many Sikh men do. A pickup truck pulls in. Today: after September 2001.

The man in the truck shot and killed Balbir Singh Sodhi. That same day he fired at other people he thought looked like the enemy, including a Lebanese American clerk and the home of an Afghan American family. When he was arrested, he said he was standing up for America. He was convicted of murder. Balbir Singh Sodhi is remembered as one of the first people killed in a hate crime after September eleventh. He had come to America from Punjab, driven a taxi, saved money with his brothers, and bought that gas station. In the months and years that followed, many Sikhs in America were attacked, insulted or treated with suspicion, most often because of the turban and beard. Now the hard and important part. It would be easy to say: this was a mistake, he wasn't Muslim. Many Sikhs, and many Sikh organizations, refuse to put it that way. They say the problem is not who the attacker got wrong. The problem is attacking anyone because of how they look or what they believe. No one deserves that, Muslim, Sikh or anyone else. That's a teaching as old as Guru Nanak, who saw the one light in every person. The Sodhi family answered with the same spirit. Balbir's brother Rana spent years speaking in schools, churches and community halls, telling his brother's story, so that people would know their Sikh neighbors. Ignorance was the soil. Knowing each other is the cure. That's the line: know your neighbor.
screen: `SHOT OUTSIDE HIS GAS STATION.` · `ATTACKED FOR HOW HE LOOKED.` · `NOT A MISTAKE: WRONG FOR ANYONE.` · `A BROTHER WHO TOLD THE STORY.` · then, large: `KNOW YOUR NEIGHBOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: gather one fact to counter a stereotype. Settle, and breathe. From everything you've learned on this path, choose one simple true thing you could tell someone about Sikhs. That the turban honors uncut hair. That Sikh means learner. That the langar feeds anyone who walks in. Say it to yourself in one sentence, the way you'd say it to a friend. Then think of one person who might need to hear it. Rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Guandhi. A neighbor, the person next door — after Balbir Singh Sodhi was killed in a hate crime in Arizona in September 2001, his family worked so neighbors would know each other.
Your line: know your neighbor. Today, learn one thing about a neighbor's faith or culture that you didn't know, by asking, reading or listening. Day three hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Sikh Americans remember Balbir Singh Sodhi each September, and many Sikh organizations run school talks, open gurdwara days and langar for neighbors so people come to know one another.

trapdoor: what you thought: he was killed because he was mistaken for someone else.
what it means: he was killed for how he looked, and many Sikhs say no one should ever be attacked for that.
what a scholar hears: groups such as the Sikh Coalition formed in the weeks after September 11, 2001, to document attacks and teach neighbors about Sikhs.
